findings.remaining_action: This closes the adjudication/refresh half of RT-16 (can now ask the venue about ONE order it suspects is ambiguous or stale) AND now feeds ReconciliationScheduler's own, already-correct escalation policy with real MEDIUM-severity divergences. STILL NOT DONE, as a deliberate scope decision made and verified this session: ConsistencyChecker is NOT wired up, because it has three separate, compounding problems that would need fixing together, not patched individually -- (1) _get_active_tenant_exchanges() returns a hardcoded empty list, so it currently checks nothing; (2) _get_exchange_positions() calls get_or_create_exchange with no credentials and calls fetch_positions(), the wrong ccxt method for a spot-only platform; (3) _handle_mismatch() trips a GLOBAL kill switch on ANY mismatch, with no severity gating at all (unlike ReconciliationScheduler's own correct, already-scoped policy). Wiring real tenant data through (1) and (2) while (3) still halts the whole platform on any noise would risk a false-positive global halt; fixing it properly needs all three addressed together with sandbox verification, which is out of scope for this pass. Also still open: no private order/fill stream is consumed anywhere, so a fill the watchdog never suspected is still invisible; execution_records are still marked COMPLETED on venue accept rather than on a confirmed fill; real sandbox certification against a live exchange remains EXTERNAL_BLOCKED (no sandbox credentials available this session), estimated 40-80h remaining by the original audit even after both fixes in this session. _get_active_tenant_exchanges() DELIBERATELY still returns [] -- enumerating real tenant/exchange pairs today, even with the three fixes above, is not safe: PositionModel (the LOCAL side of this comparison) has NO WRITER anywhere in the live/paper trading execution path (backend/position_engine.py's PositionEngine is fully built but has zero callers -- grep confirms it) -- so every tenant holding any real exchange balance would register a permanent, structural MISSING_LOCAL finding on EVERY check, forever, flooding the very reconciliation_mismatches table this session just made useful via OrderWatchdog. On top of that, PositionModel.side is long/short -- a derivatives model that does not fit this platform's spot-only, always-non-negative exposure model (RT-21's own finding on BotRunner.recovered_exposure_coins). Enabling this for real needs (a) PositionModel actually wired into the live order path (a separate, nontrivial change touching the order path, not something to bolt on under this pass) and (b) a deliberate design decision on how a spot balance maps to a long/short-shaped position row -- both out of scope here and documented, not silently dropped, in _get_active_tenant_exchanges's own docstring.

findings.title: Sign-out does not revoke the caller's session
findings.evidence: Confirmed root cause: signout built an ANON-keyed Supabase client (never authenticated as the caller) and called its plain client.auth.sign_out() -- that signs the CLIENT OBJECT'S OWN locally-tracked session out, which this client never had, so the call was always a no-op returning a false 200. The `token` parameter was accepted but never read. Fixed: client.auth.admin.sign_out(jwt=current_user['access_token'], scope='global') against a service-role client (get_service_supabase), which makes a real server-to-server revocation naming WHOSE session to end. tests/test_auth01_signout_revokes_the_real_session.py (4 tests): admin sign-out called with the caller's own token and scope='global'; no service-role client is a clean 503 not a fake success; an admin API failure is a 400; auth is still required. findings.title: Background schedulers run in every web worker
findings.evidence: Confirmed in main.py: start_reconciliation_scheduler() is called from the FastAPI lifespan startup hook, which every uvicorn/gunicorn web worker process runs independently -- so every worker built its own ReconciliationScheduler (core/reconciliation_scheduler.py) and polled the shared reconciliation_mismatches table every POLL_INTERVAL_SECONDS (30s) from N processes at once, each attempting to escalate the same mismatches and trigger the same kill switch redundantly. Checked RECON-01 first to confirm this is a DIFFERENT, already-running scheduler from ExchangeReconciliationService (RECON-01's subject, never started anywhere) -- did not touch RECON-01's deliberately-deferred leader-election/tenant-enumeration work, only this already-running one. Neither duplicated action was itself corrupted (the kill switch and the 'already-escalated' DB check are each idempotent on their own), so the real cost was DB/alerting load multiplied by N for no benefit. Fixed by adding _try_become_leader: a renewable Redis lease using the exact same primitive master_executor's execution lock and IdempotentExchangeSubmission.claim_submission already use (SET key value NX EX to win an unheld lease; a plain SET to renew one still held by the SAME instance id, checked via GET first, since a one-shot NX-only lock would make even the current leader lose and re-win the role every cycle). Fails CLOSED the same way those two already do -- redis_manager.get_client() returning None or raising answers 'not leader' rather than letting a per-process mock stand in for Redis outside development and silently reintroduce the N-way fan-out, exactly the failure mode tests/test_redis_fallback_does_not_fake_a_distributed_lock.py already guards the other two locks against. _loop now calls _poll_and_escalate only when leader. New tests/test_inf04_reconciliation_scheduler_leader_election.py (8 tests) against a fake Redis client backed by a store SHARED across instances (unlike MockRedisClient's per-process dict): exactly one of two schedulers wins leadership in the same cycle; the same leader renews rather than losing the role every cycle; a different instance cannot steal an active lease; a crashed leader's expired lease is picked up by another instance; Redis unreachable/erroring both fail closed; a non-leader cycle skips _poll_and_escalate entirely while a leader cycle runs it. Full regression: 6 existing reconciliation/health test files + test_redis_fallback_does_not_fake_a_distributed_lock.py (75 passed); test_validation_sweep.py (373 passed, 2 skipped).
findings.remaining_action: None identified for ReconciliationScheduler, the scheduler this finding's own evidence names as actually running in every worker today. RECON-01's ExchangeReconciliationService remains separately, deliberately OPEN (not started anywhere at all yet, and its own leader-election + tenant-enumeration design is explicitly deferred to a dedicated session per that finding's own remaining_action) -- this fix does not close RECON-01 and was not intended to. If another in-process scheduler is added later that also runs via the FastAPI lifespan hook, it will need its own leader check; this fix is scoped to ReconciliationScheduler alone, not a generic one-leader-per-process framework.

findings.title: Long-lived AWS keys in CI; mutable :latest tag pushed; digest fallback
findings.evidence: Confirmed all three sub-issues directly in .github/workflows/02-build.yml and 03-deploy.yml before changing anything. (1) Mutable :latest: 02-build.yml built and pushed both $ECR_REGISTRY/$ECR_REPOSITORY:$IMAGE_TAG (the commit SHA) AND $ECR_REGISTRY/$ECR_REPOSITORY:latest. Confirmed via grep that the live deploy path never reads :latest -- scripts/ecs_deploy_and_diagnose.py builds its own image_uri as f'{ECR_REGISTRY}/vyomquant-api:{IMAGE_TAG}' where IMAGE_TAG is 03-deploy.yml's own '${{ github.event.workflow_run.head_sha || github.sha }}', i.e. always the commit SHA -- so :latest was a standing mutable pointer in the registry with no current reader, but a live risk for the first future thing that pulls by tag instead of digest/SHA. Removed the :latest build+push; only the immutable SHA tag is pushed now. (2) Digest fallback: the same step computed DIGEST via `aws ecr describe-images ... || echo "$IMAGE_TAG"` -- on a describe failure this silently set image_digest to a TAG, not a digest, with no error. Grepped every workflow and script for image_digest/outputs.image_digest: nothing currently consumes it, so this had no live blast radius, but fixed it anyway since an output that lies about its own contents on failure is a trap for whatever becomes its first reader -- now fails the step with ::error:: instead of echoing a fake digest. (3) Long-lived AWS keys: both workflows authenticate via secrets.AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID/AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY through aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4 -- a standing IAM user credential, not scoped to GitHub Actions, with no expiry. NOT flipped live this pass (see remaining_action) but terraform/iam.tf now defines the OIDC provider + role a dedicated session with real AWS access needs to complete the fix: aws_iam_openid_connect_provider.github_actions (token.actions.githubusercontent.com, aud=sts.amazonaws.com) and aws_iam_role.github_actions_deploy, trusted only for this repo's main/master branches via the OIDC sub claim (terraform/variables.tf gained github_repository, default 'Narendra2212/vyomquant-saas', for that condition), with an attached policy scoped to exactly the ecr:*/ecs:*/logs:*/iam:PassRole calls 02-build.yml and scripts/ecs_deploy_and_diagnose.py actually make (enumerated by grepping every `aws ecs`/`aws ecr`/`aws logs` subcommand in both). Verified .github/workflows/02-build.yml as valid YAML (python yaml.safe_load) and terraform/iam.tf + variables.tf as valid HCL (python-hcl2 -- no terraform binary available in this sandbox for a real `terraform validate`/`plan`). Full regression: tests/test_validation_sweep.py (376 passed, 2 skipped) -- a CI/infra-config-only change touching no application code.
findings.remaining_action: Two of three sub-issues are fully fixed and need nothing further (:latest push removed; digest fallback now fails loudly instead of lying). The long-lived-keys sub-issue is NOT flipped live: the terraform role exists only as unapplied source, and 02-build.yml/03-deploy.yml still authenticate with the static IAM user keys. This was a deliberate sequencing decision, not an oversight -- switching either workflow's configure-aws-credentials step to role-to-assume before the role actually exists in AWS would break every build and deploy outright, and this sandbox has no real AWS credentials to terraform apply it with first. A dedicated session with real AWS access must, in order: (1) terraform apply the new OIDC provider + role; (2) point both workflows' configure-aws-credentials@v4 step at role-to-assume (and add permissions: id-token: write to 03-deploy.yml's jobs -- 02-build.yml already declares it, unused until now); (3) once both workflows have run green against the role at least once, delete the long-lived IAM user access key from AWS IAM and from the repo's AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID/AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY GitHub secrets. The IAM policy attached to the new role should be reviewed against this account's real IAM-boundary conventions before that apply -- it was scoped from static analysis of what the scripts call, not verified against a real AWS account.

findings.title: Security scanning gaps
findings.evidence: Confirmed the real gap before writing anything: pip-audit/npm audit/cargo-audit all already existed, but only in 04-nightly-audit.yml -- a 02:00 UTC cron plus workflow_dispatch only, never push/PR -- and every one of the three steps is marked `continue-on-error: true`, so even the nightly run never blocked anything; findings landed in an uploaded JSON artifact nobody is forced to open. Separately, 05-security.yml's existing iac-scan job scans for secrets but only under terraform/ and aerora_quant_platform/infrastructure/ -- that job's own SC-29 comment names the reason (deliberate fake-credential fixtures in tests/ would trip a repo-wide scan) and the fix ('needs an ignore file written first'). Added two new jobs to 05-security.yml (which already runs on push/PR to main/master plus a nightly cron): (1) secret-scan-repo-wide -- grepped the whole tree for the exact patterns Trivy's secret scanner looks for (PEM BEGIN markers, AKIA.../sk_test_/sk_live_ shapes) to enumerate every deliberate fixture rather than guess: exactly 11 files, all under tests/, none in backend_app/ or scripts/. Trivy's skip-files input names those 11 specifically (not all of tests/), so new test files stay covered by default. Blocks on CRITICAL/HIGH. (2) dependency-audit -- installs the real production requirements-cpu.txt, runs pip-audit against that installed environment with --ignore-vuln for exactly DEP-01's own currently-irreducible residual advisory IDs (re-confirmed this session with a real pip-audit run, see DEP-01's own evidence: PYSEC-2026-161/248/249/2280/2281 starlette, PYSEC-2026-3447 setuptools, PYSEC-2026-1805 protobuf -- python-dotenv's former PYSEC-2026-2270 is NOT ignored, since this session's prior commit 8384443 already closed it); verified locally against this session's venv that the exact ignore list leaves zero findings (`pip-audit --ignore-vuln <all seven>` -> 'No known vulnerabilities found, 14 ignored', exit 0). Then runs `npm audit --audit-level=high --omit=dev` in algo22-terminal, blocking, verified locally against the real lockfile -> 'found 0 vulnerabilities' today, matching DEP-01's own prior finding. pip-audit has no severity-threshold flag (unlike Trivy's `severity:` input), so this gate is 'block on anything with a fix available except this explicit, reviewed list' rather than a HIGH+ threshold -- documented as a deliberate, honest deviation from the remaining_action's literal 'blocking on HIGH+' wording, not a silent one. NOT independently verified end-to-end in a real GitHub Actions runner: no trivy binary and no GitHub Actions execution available in this sandbox (the same limitation CI-03's own ledger entry already records for Trivy-related CI changes) -- skip-files/scanners:secret as trivy-action inputs could not be exercised against a real trivy binary here, only the YAML syntax (python yaml.safe_load) and the two commands that run outside trivy (pip-audit, npm audit) were actually executed. Full regression: tests/test_validation_sweep.py (376 passed, 2 skipped) -- a CI-config-only change touching no application code.
findings.remaining_action: Two of three named gaps are addressed (full-tree secret scan now exists and blocks; pip-audit/npm audit now block on push/PR, not just a non-blocking nightly cron). NOT verified against a real GitHub Actions run -- this sandbox has neither a trivy binary nor GitHub Actions execution, so the trivy-action `skip-files`/`scanners` inputs used by the new secret-scan-repo-wide job are unverified beyond YAML syntax; review its first real run and be ready to adjust the input names/format if trivy-action's actual schema differs from what this pass assumed. 'Pin actions by SHA' (the third gap this finding names) is NOT attempted: every workflow in this repo pins third-party actions by tag (@v4, @v0.36.0, etc), not commit SHA, and this sandbox has no GitHub API access to the ~6 distinct action repositories involved (actions/checkout, actions/setup-python, actions/setup-node, aws-actions/*, aquasecurity/trivy-action, docker/*) to resolve each tag to its real commit SHA -- guessing a SHA wrong would silently pin to the wrong commit or simply fail to resolve, and this ledger's own established discipline is to never guess at unverifiable infrastructure values. A dedicated session with that API access should resolve and pin all of them together in one pass (so the whole fleet moves at once, not piecemeal).

findings.title: Refunds do not revoke plan entitlement; webhook idempotency lives only in Redis for 24h
findings.evidence: This finding has two halves; confirmed the first was already closed. (1) 'Refunds do not revoke plan entitlement': backend_app/routers/billing.py::_revoke_plan_for_refunded_razorpay_payment (BILL-01, VERIFIED_FIXED earlier this session) is called from the Razorpay refund.processed handler and revokes a fully-refunded plan, gateway-confirmed. Razorpay is the only live payment provider this deployment bills plans through (src/pages/Billing.jsx documents no live Stripe secret exists; every Stripe-only endpoint 500s by design), so BILL-01 already covers the real production path; not re-done here. (2) 'Webhook idempotency lives only in Redis for 24h': confirmed by reading both webhook handlers in billing.py: a 'processing' key (60s TTL) transitioning to 'completed' (86400s TTL) was the SOLE idempotency record. core/cache/redis_manager.py is deliberately fail-soft (every method swallows its own exception and returns a falsy default), so a Redis outage during the initial check silently read as 'not a duplicate' and the handler proceeded to reprocess a real duplicate delivery undetected -- and even with Redis healthy, a redelivery more than 24h after the first (both providers redeliver for days; an operator can manually resend an old webhook from either dashboard for reconciliation) found no record at all once the 'completed' key expired. Fixed by adding a DURABLE claim layered UNDERNEATH the existing Redis fast path (not a replacement -- preserves every existing Redis-based test's assertions unchanged): new migration backend_app/migrations/045_sec03_durable_webhook_events.sql creates public.webhook_events (UNIQUE (provider, event_id), service-role only, RLS enabled, no anon/authenticated grants), applied and verified idempotent against a real local PostgreSQL 16 instance (CREATE then re-CREATE, both clean). New core/webhook_idempotency.py (acquire_webhook_processing/mark_webhook_completed/release_webhook_processing) uses Postgres's own unique-constraint enforcement as the atomicity primitive -- no TTL to outlive. A 'processing' row older than PROCESSING_STALE_AFTER_SECONDS (60s, matching the old Redis TTL) is reclaimable, preserving the original crash-safety property. Wired into BOTH webhook handlers (Stripe and Razorpay) at every existing acquire/complete/release point, additively: Redis's own check still runs and still refuses first (unchanged, so the pre-existing tests/test_webhook_duplicate_delivery_real_redis.py -- 646 lines of real-Redis keyspace-split-proof engineering -- needed zero changes and still passes, gated as before on AERORA_TEST_REDIS_URL); the durable claim is a second, independent gate immediately after. Not configured (get_service_supabase_async() returns None -- the normal DEV_MODE/local/test shape) defers entirely to Redis rather than refusing every webhook; configured but a call raising (a real outage) fails closed. New tests/test_sec03_durable_webhook_idempotency.py (9 tests, against a fake PostgREST table reproducing real unique-constraint conflict/filter semantics): fresh acquire succeeds; a second concurrent acquire is refused; a completed delivery is refused with NO TTL (re-checked 3 times); a stale processing row is reclaimed (the crash-recovery property); release deletes a processing row (immediate retry, no staleness wait) but never touches an already-completed row (a bug this test caught and that was fixed in the test's own fake, not application code); not-configured defers to Redis rather than refusing everything; configured-but-unreachable fails closed; a static source check confirms billing.py calls all three functions at both handlers. Full regression (migration_tooling, db01_provisioning_order, webhook_duplicate_delivery_real_redis, billing_e2e, sec02_razorpay_webhook_reconciles_order, billing_hardening_and_failure_recovery_audit, validation_sweep, route_contract -- 545 tests) clean except the 2 unrelated pre-existing billing failures already confirmed earlier this session.

findings.title: No account deletion or data export
findings.evidence: Confirmed by grep (delete_account/account_deletion/data_export/export_user_data/anonymize) that neither feature existed anywhere in this codebase. New backend/account_lifecycle.py adds both, deliberately scoped to what can be built and verified safely from this sandbox without a real Postgres instance. export_account_data(supabase, user_id) reads every category this module knows how to read directly through the request-scoped (RLS-respecting) client -- profile, strategies, backtests, marketplace subscriptions/listings, settlements, and paper trading sessions (via the existing paper_repository.list_sessions) -- with connected exchange NAMES listed via APIKeyVault.list_connected_exchanges but decrypted API credentials themselves never exported. Each category reports its own ok/error so one failing table does not abort the export. delete_account(supabase, user_id, user) is deliberately NOT a physical cascade-delete across this repository's ~58 tables -- auditing which may legally and safely be hard-deleted without a real Postgres instance to verify against is exactly the kind of repo-wide change this session has consistently declined to improvise (the same reasoning TENANT-01's FORCE RLS wiring and RECON-01's leader election were left to a dedicated session over, cross-referenced directly in the module's own docstring). Instead it composes existing, already-tested primitives: stops every live deployment (strategy_lifecycle.stop_deployments_for_reason, the same Requirement 20.9 path the kill switch already uses), stops every RUNNING/PAUSED paper session (paper_session_service.stop_session, called the way it is already designed to be called without a live feed/task handle), revokes every connected exchange's API keys (APIKeyVault.delete_exchange_keys), and anonymises the profile's PII fields while setting is_frozen=True -- the same flag core.dependencies.get_current_user already enforces as a 403 everywhere, achieving the functional equivalent of account deletion with no new column and no migration. The profile anonymisation step is the one allowed to raise (a row that cannot be updated means the account is not deleted); the other three steps are best-effort and individually reported. Two new routes: GET /api/user/account/export and DELETE /api/user/account, the latter requiring an exact confirmation phrase in the body (422 otherwise) since there is no undo for the PII anonymisation. New tests/test_priv01_account_export_and_deletion.py (9 tests): export reads every direct table scoped to the user and never includes decrypted credentials; a failing category does not abort the export; deletion stops deployments, stops only RUNNING/PAUSED sessions (not CREATED/STOPPED), revokes every connected exchange's keys, anonymises the profile; deletion raises when the profile update matches no row; one exchange failing to revoke does not stop profile anonymisation; the export route requires auth; the delete route rejects a wrong confirmation phrase and succeeds with the exact one. Registered the new DELETE route in test_validation_sweep.py's exhaustive MUTATING_ROUTES list (its own self-enforcing coverage check caught the omission on first run). Full regression: test_user_router.py + test_validation_sweep.py (387 passed, 2 skipped).
findings.remaining_action: This closes 'no account deletion or data export' with a scoped, safe implementation, not an exhaustive one. Deletion anonymises PII and revokes live resources rather than physically deleting historical strategy/backtest/settlement/paper-trading rows -- a deliberate choice (see evidence) to retain financial/audit history rather than risk an unverified cascade-delete across ~58 tables from a sandbox with no real Postgres instance. If the product's actual legal/compliance requirement is physical erasure of ALL historical rows (stronger than anonymisation + access revocation), that is a dedicated-session undertaking requiring a disposable Postgres instance to verify against, matching TENANT-01/RECON-01's own documented reasoning for similar repo-wide changes. The export likewise covers the categories this module reads directly and says so in its own response ('contact support for any category not listed here') rather than claiming completeness across all 58 tables. Supabase Auth's own user record (login credentials, separate from this codebase's profiles table) is not touched by delete_account -- is_frozen=True already blocks every API call regardless of whether the underlying Auth identity could still technically log in, which this session judged sufficient without calling Supabase's destructive, irreversible admin delete-user API from an unverified pass.

findings.title: Privilege-hardening backstop does not detect RLS-disabled customer tables
findings.evidence: Confirmed the defect by reading scripts/post_migration_validation.py section 3 ("VALIDATING RLS STATUS"): it checked rowsecurity only for tables already named in the required_tables list defined at the top of the same function -- the same list section 1 checks for existence. A table a later migration grants anon or authenticated a privilege on (Supabase grants most new tables a default privilege shape automatically) but never gets ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY would not be examined at all unless someone also remembered to add its name to this list -- the exact gap the title names. Separately, the script never called sys.exit(1) despite importing sys, so even a FAILED line printed to stdout left the process exiting 0. Fixed both: fetch_privileged_tables_without_rls(cur) now asks the catalog directly (pg_tables joined against information_schema.table_privileges for grantee IN ('anon','authenticated')) for every table either role can touch, with no table name hardcoded anywhere; evaluate_privilege_hardening(rows) is the pure decision half (same fetch/evaluate split already used in scripts/verify_rls.py), and validate_production_db() now returns that result, with __main__ calling sys.exit(1) when it fails. VERIFIED AGAINST A REAL POSTGRESQL 16 SERVER (this session's own local instance): created a table named db03_brand_new_customer_table_not_on_any_list -- confirmed absent from required_tables by inspecting validate_production_db's own source -- granted authenticated SELECT on it with RLS left disabled, and proved the new check finds it anyway (fetch_privileged_tables_without_rls returns it; evaluate_privilege_hardening fails). Negative controls: enabling RLS on that same table makes the check pass; a table with no anon/authenticated grant at all is never flagged even with RLS disabled (service-only tables are a normal, intentional configuration). New tests/test_db03_privilege_hardening_detects_untracked_tables_postgres.py (4 tests, real Postgres) and tests/test_db03_privilege_hardening_pure_logic.py (5 tests, no database) all passed. tests/test_migration_tooling.py (36 tests, pre-existing, covers this same file's import-of-os regression) still passes.
findings.remaining_action: Not wired into any CI workflow (grepped .github/ -- no match), and was not before this fix either; it remains a manually-run script. A dedicated session should add it as a CI gate run against a disposable Postgres instance, or against staging before a production migration is promoted. Sections 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 of the same script (table existence, column existence, RPC existence, security-definer check, metadata export) were not touched -- this finding names only the RLS/privilege check's detection gap, not those checks' own exit-code behavior.

The router module and the backend/distributed_execution/ package are explicitly NOT deleted/archived -- several existing tests import them directly by path to pin the orchestrator's unstarted state, and deleting them would break that coverage for no safety benefit (the mount, not the module, was the reachable surface). Full targeted regression (test_execution_paths_that_claim_an_exchange.py 25/25, test_validation_sweep.py 489 total with only the 2 pre-existing unrelated billing failures confirmed via git stash comparison, test_schema_table_reference_drift.py, tests/regression/ with only 6 pre-existing unrelated baseline failures also confirmed via git stash comparison) all clean.

findings.title: Supabase anon JWT committed in six scripts
findings.evidence: Grepped the repo for the JWT literal and confirmed the title's own count: exactly six scripts/*.py files hardcoded the identical real Supabase anon JWT for this project (ref wrkexcjqnidkdrayhlsi, role anon, committed to git) -- verify_authenticated_production.py, battery_20_samples.py, run_production_browser_forensic_audit.py, verify_production_browser_final.py, generate_browser_console_baseline.py (identical SUPABASE_ANON_KEY = "eyJ..." line in all five), and test_currency_repro.py (same literal, assigned via an unconditional os.environ[...] = ... instead). All six now read SUPABASE_ANON_KEY from the environment (test_currency_repro.py via setdefault on SUPABASE_URL plus a presence check on SUPABASE_ANON_KEY, so a caller's own value still wins) and exit with a clear message naming the missing variable when it is unset, rather than silently falling back to the committed credential. New tests/test_sec06_no_hardcoded_supabase_jwt_in_scripts.py (187 tests): a JWT-shaped-literal regex scan across every file in scripts/ (not just the six named, so a seventh script reintroducing the pattern is caught the same way) finds none; each of the six named scripts is executed as a subprocess with SUPABASE_ANON_KEY unset and asserted to exit non-zero naming that variable (three of the six import playwright at module level before anything this fix touches -- those three skip gracefully, not fail, in an environment where playwright is not installed, rather than reporting a false negative about the env-var guard); and a static source check confirms each reads os.environ.get("SUPABASE_ANON_KEY") rather than some other hardcoded source. The subprocess tests deliberately never set a real or fake key and let the scripts proceed -- five of the six scripts make a real network call to a live production endpoint shortly after the env-var check, and this test suite must not issue those requests on every run.
findings.remaining_action: SUPABASE_URL (the project's own Supabase domain, not a secret -- it is also decodable from inside the JWT's own claims, which is what made this an anon-key finding and not a URL-confidentiality one) was deliberately left hardcoded in the five scripts that had it as a bare constant; SEC-06 and its remediation note ("Read from env") name the JWT specifically. Credential rotation for the leaked anon key itself (now that it has been in git history) is an operator action this sandboxed session cannot perform; anon keys are designed to be client-exposed and are gated entirely by RLS, so this is a hygiene/policy fix, not a live-exploit fix.

findings.title: Paper session loops run in the web process on the caller's one-hour JWT and die silently
findings.evidence: Root cause fixed: backend_app/routers/paper_trading.py::start_paper_session now resolves get_service_supabase() (non-expiring) and hands it to _session_loop_spawner instead of the caller RLS-scoped client built from user["access_token"] (a Supabase JWT expiring in ~1 hour). findings.title: A paper fill is seven separate PostgREST writes with no transaction and no repair
findings.evidence: Read paper_simulator.apply_fill's own extensive docstring ('THE WRITES, AND THE ORDERING THE MISSING TRANSACTION FORCES') before changing anything: the 7-write sequence is already a deliberate, carefully-reasoned design -- the fill row is written first as the idempotency anchor so a crash before the account UPDATE can be RESUMED rather than lost or double-applied, and a crash past that point is reported as PaperConcurrencyExhausted(partial_write=True) and never retried, because a retry would double-apply money. The docstring states plainly that 'Requirement 24.6's single transaction is not achievable over this transport'. This is a considered tradeoff, not an oversight, and this fix does not revisit it -- doing so would mean second-guessing a documented architectural decision without understanding the full 'not achievable over this transport' constraint, which is exactly the kind of risky, superficial-looking-but-actually-regressive change this session's mandate is to avoid. The real, fixable gap was the 'no repair' half: a partial-write failure's detail reaches only the one HTTP caller of the one request that hit it, with nothing durable recorded, so a dropped connection or an inattentive caller left the affected session undiscoverable afterward. paper_replay.replay already exists (built for Requirement 15.4's audit trail) and independently rebuilds a session's final state from its append-only event/order log, but was unused outside its own module and tests -- there was no counterpart projecting the LIVE rows in a comparable shape, which Reconstruction.as_dict's own docstring anticipates ('a reconstruction and a projection of the stored rows... compare with a bare =='). Added backend/paper/paper_reconciliation.py: project_stored_state reads the live rows through the same paper_repository functions every other caller uses, in exactly the shape tests/test_paper_replay.py's own _stored/_reconstructed pair already uses to prove a healthy session's replay-fidelity (reused that contract rather than inventing a second opinion about what 'the stored state' means -- proved byte-identical to it in a new test). reconcile_session calls replay.replay, projects both sides, and reports which of 7 subjects (balances, realized_pnl, orders, fills, positions, closed_trades, equity_series) disagree. Writes nothing; returns None for both 'no such session' and 'another tenant's session', the same non-disclosure replay itself gives. Wired to GET /api/admin/paper/sessions/{id}/reconcile in routers/admin.py, gated by get_admin_user (matching this file's own stated /kill-switch reasoning: reading agreement with a log is strictly weaker than anything that could change it) and reading through the service-role client so an admin can reconcile any user's session. New tests/test_paper05_reconciliation.py (7 tests, against the real production-loop fixture test_paper_replay.py already trusts): clean session reconciles with zero mismatches; project_stored_state is byte-identical to that file's own _stored helper on the identical rows; a tampered balance, order and position are each caught under the right subject; unknown/other-tenant sessions answer None; nothing is written. New tests/test_paper05_reconciliation_endpoint.py (5 tests): admin-gated, reports clean/dirty end-to-end, 404s identically for unknown and other-tenant sessions. Full regression: tests/test_paper_replay.py + test_task_27_session_service.py (246 passed); test_role_granularity_and_audit.py + 4 other admin-router test files (127 passed, 1 pre-existing unrelated Redis-dependent kill-switch failure confirmed via git-stash comparison); test_validation_sweep.py (373 passed, 2 skipped).
findings.remaining_action: This closes the 'no repair' half only; the 'no transaction' half is a documented, considered tradeoff (see apply_fill's own docstring) that this pass deliberately did not revisit -- doing so would mean moving apply_fill/submit into a single-transaction RPC against the team's own stated reasoning for why that is 'not achievable over this transport', which is a larger, riskier change to the live money-movement write path and is out of scope here. The new endpoint is on-demand, not a nightly job: nothing in this sandbox can verify a real cron schedule, so scheduling GET /api/admin/paper/sessions/{id}/reconcile (or a sweep across every session with a known partial_write incident) as a recurring job is the remaining infra-level action. Persisting partial_write incidents to a durable table (so a sweep can target just the affected sessions instead of every one) would close that and is also not attempted here.

findings.title: Any access_token in the URL hash becomes the session (login CSRF)
findings.evidence: Confirmed the defect directly in algo22-terminal/src/App.jsx: getEffectiveToken() (read by both AuthGuard and GuestGuard, so on every protected and every guest-only route) checked window.location.hash for access_token= on ANY path and, if not demonstrably expired, silently adopted it into sessionStorage -- a non-expired token proves only that Supabase signed it for SOMEONE, not that it was issued to this browser or that this page load is a legitimate redirect. PasswordRecoveryHandler's own non-recovery access_token= branch had the identical defect, unconditionally (storing the token before even checking the path, let alone expiry). Confirmed Google OAuth (signInWithOAuth) and magic-link OTP (signInWithOtp) are both real, offered sign-in methods (AuthPage.jsx), so this hash-handling could not simply be deleted. Confirmed config.js::getAuthRedirectUrl is the SINGLE redirect target Supabase is ever told to use for every OTP/sign-up/resend/OAuth call site (AUTH_REDIRECT_PATH = '/app/dashboard'), and that no resetPasswordForEmail call with an explicit redirectTo exists anywhere in src/ (so the recovery email's landing path is NOT controlled by this frontend and cannot be safely allowlisted). Fixed by requiring window.location.pathname to be one of the paths Supabase is actually ever told to redirect to (AUTH_REDIRECT_PATH/signin/signup/root) before either call site honours a hash access_token; also added the missing expiry check to PasswordRecoveryHandler's two branches. New tests/unit/authHashLandingPath.test.jsx (4 tests, vitest): the allowlist accepts exactly the four legitimate paths and rejects an arbitrary in-app page; a direct exercise of getEffectiveToken() proves a hash token on a disallowed path is never stored or returned, and the identical token on the real redirect path IS adopted (proving this narrows, not removes, the feature). Pre-existing auth suites (auth_otp/auth_oauth/authRedirectOrigin, 52 tests) still pass unchanged.
findings.remaining_action: This narrows the attack from 'any page in the app' to 'the one path Supabase is told to redirect to', but does NOT make the underlying implicit OAuth/magic-link flow itself CSRF-proof: an attacker can still craft a link landing on AUTH_REDIRECT_PATH itself (https://<app>/app/dashboard#access_token=<attacker's own valid token>) and a victim clicking it still adopts the attacker's session. The complete fix is PKCE (flowType: 'pkce' on the Supabase client), which binds the callback to a locally-held code_verifier an attacker cannot forge -- but switching flowType changes the redirect format for every auth path (OAuth, magic link, sign-up, AND the password-recovery email this frontend does not even control the redirect for) and is a live-Supabase-project-config change this sandboxed session has no live project or OAuth provider credentials to test end-to-end. Explicitly not attempted, to avoid shipping an untested change to the only path into the product. The type=recovery branch's landing path is not allowlisted at all, for the stated reason (this frontend never sets its redirectTo), and remains exposed to the same class of attack without narrowing.

findings.title: The web app is served without a Content-Security-Policy
findings.evidence: Confirmed by reading algo22-terminal/index.html and .github/workflows/06-frontend-deploy.yml: this SPA is built by Vite and synced straight to an S3 bucket behind CloudFront (no origin server at request time, unlike the API's own SecurityHeadersMiddleware in backend_app/main.py, which already sends a tightened nonce+hash CSP but only on backend-served responses) -- index.html carried no CSP at all, meta or header, and could not easily be given one without weakening it: three inline <script> blocks (local-dev detection, a Sentry loader, a GA/Clarity loader) would have forced 'unsafe-inline' into script-src the moment a CSP was added, which defeats most of what a CSP is for. Fixed both problems together. (1) The three inline scripts moved verbatim (same isDummy/local-detection/loader logic, now reading import.meta.env.VITE_* instead of index.html's %VITE_X% token substitution -- equivalent at build time, Vite's native mechanism either way) into algo22-terminal/src/bootstrap.js, a same-origin ES module loaded via <script type="module" src="/src/bootstrap.js"> ahead of main.jsx -- already covered by script-src 'self' with no extra grant needed. (2) index.html now carries <meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy"> with script-src 'self' plus only the origins this build actually loads scripts from (confirmed by grep of src/: js.sentry-cdn.com, www.googletagmanager.com, www.clarity.ms, checkout.razorpay.com for the one real payment path this platform has -- Stripe origins deliberately excluded, since src/pages/Billing.jsx documents this deployment has no live Stripe secret and every Stripe-only endpoint 500s by design) -- no unsafe-inline, no unsafe-eval anywhere in the policy. connect-src covers every API-hostname topology the deploy workflow's own allow-list names (same-origin CloudFront proxy, api.vyomquant.in, or the raw CloudFront domain) plus the wildcarded Supabase, Sentry, Clarity and GA hosts the app actually calls. A meta-tag CSP cannot carry frame-ancestors/sandbox/report-uri (browsers ignore those three outside an HTTP header per the HTML spec) -- documented in index.html's own comment and left to INF-02 (terraform does not describe the production deployment; a CloudFront response-headers policy is the real fix for that gap, and this session has no AWS credentials to apply one even if terraform described the live distribution). New tests/unit/csp_fe02.test.js (11 tests): the CSP meta tag exists; script-src is 'self' plus https-only named origins with no unsafe-inline/unsafe-eval and no directive left empty; every remaining <script> tag in index.html either names a same-origin src or is the non-executable application/ld+json block (browsers do not run it as script and CSP's script-src does not gate it); bootstrap.js loads before main.jsx in document order; bootstrap.js's isDummyValue/detectLocal/runBootstrap reproduce the exact old inline-script behaviour (dummy/placeholder/test/unset id -> harmless local-only stub and no third-party script injected; a real-looking id -> the real Sentry/GA/Clarity loader script injected with that id). `npm run build` with the real Vite config still produces a working dist/index.html carrying the CSP meta tag and zero occurrences of VITE_SENTRY_DSN/VITE_GA_TRACKING_ID/VITE_CLARITY_PROJECT_ID (confirming the token substitution moved to bootstrap.js's bundled output correctly, verified by grepping the emitted entry chunk for __VQ_LOCAL__/clarity.ms/sentry-cdn, all present).
findings.remaining_action: This closes the "served without a CSP" gap in the one place this session can reach (the committed index.html). NOT done: a CloudFront response-headers policy or ALB header (the HTTP-header form of CSP, which alone can add frame-ancestors for real clickjacking protection and survives even if a future edit strips the meta tag) -- that is infrastructure this session has no AWS credentials to touch and that INF-02 already records as undescribed by the repo's own terraform. The remediation note's 'attach WAF, enable logging' half is unchanged for the same reason.

findings.title: The market-data quality validator's default thresholds reject almost all real-shaped market data
findings.evidence: Confirmed the defect exactly as named, and traced its real blast radius: OutlierDetector._z_score_filter/_iqr_filter (reached by default -- ValidationConfig.outlier_method defaults to Z_SCORE) computed their test against the RAW price/volume LEVEL of the whole window, then rejected the ENTIRE window on a single violation. market_data_contract.quality_report, strategy_operations, strategy_service and training_worker all REUSE this exact validator per their own docstrings -- this is not dead code, it sits on real production paths. Confirmed empirically (not just by reading): a realistic trending-price + log-normal-volume series (900 bars, the platform's typical window size) was rejected by the pre-fix z-score-on-levels check on every one of several random seeds tried, while the existing test suite's own 'clean, accepted' fixture (tests/test_feed_state_and_data_quality.py's _pool()) is explicitly documented as a bounded SINE WAVE rather than anything resembling real market data, specifically to dodge this exact bug -- independent confirmation the defect is real and already known-about well enough to be worked around rather than fixed. Root cause: price and volume levels are both non-stationary (price trends/drifts, volume is approximately log-normal) by construction, so a z-score/IQR test against a non-stationary series' own mean/quantiles measures 'how far this point is from a mean the trend/burst itself moved', unrelated to whether any individual bar is actually anomalous. FIX: switched both _z_score_filter and _iqr_filter to bar-to-bar LOG-RETURNS (log(x_t/x_(t-1))) for close AND volume -- the standard transform that makes a trending/multiplicative series approximately stationary, which these tests require to mean anything. Percent-change returns were tried first and empirically still left volume's heavy right tail (ordinary volume bursts are large MULTIPLICATIVE swings) fat enough to trip the z-score on realistic data (2 violations in 30 seeds); log-returns resolved it completely (0/30). Also raised z_score_threshold 3.0->5.0 and iqr_multiplier 1.5->3.0 (both env-overridable via MARKET_DATA_Z_SCORE_THRESHOLD / MARKET_DATA_IQR_MULTIPLIER): rejecting a whole window on ANY single point beyond a per-comparison threshold has a false-positive rate that RISES WITH WINDOW SIZE regardless of what it's computed over -- for a 900-bar window, a per-point threshold calibrated for a single comparison (3 sigma / 1.5xIQR) is tripped by chance alone far more often than not; this is a general multiple-comparisons argument, not a dataset-specific calibration, and both new values were empirically verified (across 25-30 independent random seeds per method) to clear realistic trending+bursty-volume windows while STILL catching a genuine single-bar 50x price spike. Investigated the third remediation item ('make the gap threshold interval-aware') and found it already true of the current code, just not of what the ledger note assumed: GapHandler.handle's actual gap DETECTION already derives its threshold from the timeframe (`expected_diff = timedelta(minutes=_timeframe_to_minutes(timeframe)); gaps = time_diffs > expected_diff * 1.5`) -- the `max_gap_minutes` PARAMETER the caller passes in (ValidationConfig.max_gap_minutes, fixed at 5.0) is dead code, immediately overwritten by the measured gap value before it is ever read. Not a gap in this codebase's current behaviour, just an unused/confusingly-named parameter; left as-is since removing a dead parameter is outside this finding's scope and touches a shared signature. New tests/test_data02_outlier_detection_on_returns_not_levels.py (39 tests): 25 independent random seeds of realistic trending-price + bursty-volume data accepted (previously rejected); a genuine single-bar 50x spike still rejected; the existing sine-wave clean/spike fixtures still behave exactly as before (both directions, independently re-verified here); the same two properties for the non-default IQR method. Full regression: new suite + tests/test_feed_state_and_data_quality.py + tests/test_market_data_contract.py + tests/test_validation_sweep.py (542 tests) clean except pre-existing, unrelated EmptyCategoryError collection errors (confirmed pre-existing/unrelated repeatedly this session) and the 2 pre-existing billing failures already confirmed earlier this session.
findings.remaining_action: The two threshold VALUES (z_score_threshold=5.0, iqr_multiplier=3.0) are principled, empirically-verified-against-synthetic-data defaults, not a fit against this platform's own real historical return distributions -- this sandbox has no such data. The original audit's own remediation note separated 'validate on returns/log-returns' (done, this session) from 'widen or recalibrate thresholds against real historical distributions' (NOT done -- needs a session with access to real market data to fine-tune beyond the general multiple-comparisons correction applied here). Both new constants are env-overridable so this can happen without a code change.

findings.evidence: Confirmed the exact mechanism before fixing it: backend_app/backend/training_worker.py's TrainingWorker.claim_training_job performs an atomic `SET status='RUNNING' ... WHERE id = :id AND status = 'QUEUED'` transition and TrainingWorker.start()/process_iteration poll for and run such jobs -- but that module's own run_worker() docstring documents that it is deliberately never started from main.py (Requirement 16.6 / TrainingIsolator's own docstring: training must run in a separate process so a fitting job can never share the API process's interpreter, saturate Redis, or block order/execution handling), and until this fix nothing ran it as that separate process in production, so a submitted training job stayed QUEUED forever. docker-compose.yml already runs it (`python -m backend_app.backend.training_worker`, confirmed by inspection) for local dev, which is why this finding's own title specifically says 'no PRODUCTION task definition' -- the gap was in terraform/ecs.tf, not everywhere. Added test_training_worker_is_now_hosted_ops_train_01 to that same file, asserting directly against terraform/ecs.tf's own text. Verified as a real regression test, not a tautology: git-stashed just the terraform/ecs.tf change and reran this one test, which failed with the expected message; restored the fix and reran, green. Full regression: tests/test_worker_deployment_coverage.py (7 passed, 1 xfailed -- pre-existing, unrelated ReconciliationWorker gap) + tests/test_validation_sweep.py (376 passed, 2 skipped). terraform/ecs.tf parses as valid HCL (python-hcl2; no terraform binary available in this sandbox for a real plan/validate against AWS's Fargate cpu/memory combo table, so 2048/8192 is a known-valid pair from memory, not verified against a live provider schema here).

Also unverified here: the 2048 cpu / 8192 memory Fargate combination is a textbook-valid pair from memory, not checked against a live `terraform plan`/`validate` or AWS's current Fargate task-size table, so review it on apply. Separately, no alerting exists yet for a training job stuck QUEUED beyond some bound even once the worker is running (e.g. the worker crashes and ECS keeps restarting it into a bad state) -- out of scope for this pass, which only closes the 'nothing runs this process' gap the title names.

findings.title: Walk-forward analysis does not actually fit per-window parameters, and several of its reported figures are hardcoded placeholders
findings.evidence: Confirmed by reading run_walk_forward_analysis: self._get_best_parameters(self._optimization_history) was called ONCE before the loop and the resulting fixed parameter set was evaluated on every window's train AND test period -- a fixed strategy re-run on rolling windows, not walk-forward analysis. Investigating this surfaced a more fundamental, previously untracked defect (filed and fixed separately as BT-02, commit 29e319d): BacktestRuntime.run_backtest never used start_date/end_date to select data at all, so every window's backtest ran on byte-identical 'most recent bars' regardless of its own dates, which would have made even a correct per-window fit numerically meaningless. Fixed run_walk_forward_analysis (depends on BT-02) by adding _optimize_on_window: a copy of the caller's config with parameters[start_date/end_date] overridden to the window's own train period, dispatched through the same search method (_grid_search/_random_search/_bayesian_optimization/_genetic_algorithm) the caller chose, with the window's own trials kept OUT of self._optimization_history so one window cannot leak into another's fit or into the whole-period benchmark (the OPT-03-shaped cross-contamination, reintroduced inside one engine instance if not guarded against). Also fixed the three hardcoded report figures the finding names: _run_buy_hold_benchmark (was the literal total_return_pct=50.0/sharpe_ratio=1.0/max_drawdown=20.0 for every call) now fetches the strategy's own symbol/timeframe over the same window via BT-02's since_ms/until_ms and computes all three from the closes actually fetched, reporting computed=False/None rather than a fabricated number when the fetch fails; _calculate_beta (was the literal 1.0) now computes cov(strategy_returns, benchmark_returns)/var(benchmark_returns) from both backtests' own return series, returning None rather than 0.0/1.0 when there are too few paired observations or the benchmark has zero variance; complexity score (was the literal 0.8) now scales with the strategy's own tunable-parameter count (1.0 at zero parameters, 0.0 at a documented 10-parameter cap), matching the 'higher is better' convention every other component of the weighted score already uses. New tests/test_opt02_walk_forward_fits_per_window_and_report_figures_are_real.py (10 tests) against a deterministic, parameter- and window-dependent fake backtest_runtime: different windows provably choose different winning parameters (not merely 'ran without crashing'); the fitted parameters carry unchanged from train to test; two windows' calls carry two different date ranges (the BT-02 dependency, checked directly); buy & hold computes a real return/Sharpe/drawdown from a controlled price series and reports not-computed on empty data; beta computes exactly (2.0 for a strategy whose returns are exactly 2x the benchmark's) and is None on zero variance or too few observations; alpha/beta are both None together when the benchmark could not be measured; complexity varies from 1.0 to 0.0 with parameter count. One real bug the test suite itself caught before commit: the first _calculate_beta draft mixed np.cov's sample covariance (ddof=1) with np.var's population variance (ddof=0), scaling every beta by N/(N-1) for no reason -- caught because the exactly-2.0 test came back 2.4, fixed by aligning both to ddof=1. Full regression: test_save_performs_no_backtest.py + test_opt01_optimize_config_field_name.py + test_strategy_analysis_endpoint_accuracy.py + test_opt03_optimization_engine_is_not_a_shared_singleton.py + test_bt02_backtest_honors_requested_date_range.py (100 passed, 1 pre-existing unrelated import-pin failure confirmed via git-stash comparison to predate this change entirely); test_validation_sweep.py (373 passed, 2 skipped).
findings.remaining_action: None identified at the code level for the two defects this finding names. The fix credits two commits: 29e319d (BT-02, the data-range prerequisite) and be82e3d (this finding's own per-window fitting and report-figure fixes). The validation_method field on OptimizationConfig (TIME_SERIES_CV/BLOCKED_CV/ROLLING_VALIDATION/WALK_FORWARD) is still read only for a log line in run_walk_forward_analysis and does not select a different windowing or fitting strategy -- that is a separate, smaller gap this pass did not scope in, since the finding's own title and remaining_action named only the per-window fitting and the hardcoded figures.

findings.title: Optimization engine is a process-wide singleton that leaks one tenant's best parameters into another tenant's walk-forward/sensitivity results
findings.evidence: Confirmed by reading backend_app/backend/optimization_engine.py::get_optimization_engine and backend_app/backend/backtest_runtime.py::get_backtest_runtime: both are plain module-level singletons (global _x; if _x is None: _x = X(); return _x). Grepped every call site in the repo (exactly two): backend_app/routers/strategy_operations.py's POST /strategies/{id}/optimize and backend_app/routers/strategies.py's POST /walk-forward both called them directly, so every tenant's call shared the SAME OptimizationEngine instance and therefore the SAME _optimization_history list -- every one of run_walk_forward_analysis/run_sensitivity_analysis/run_monte_carlo_simulation/run_benchmark_comparison reads its 'best parameters' back via self._get_best_parameters(self._optimization_history), so a tenant whose call overlapped or ran back-to-back with another tenant's in the same process could have had that tenant's optimization results folded into their own. The shared backtest_runtime singleton compounded it: constructed once with the class defaults ($10,000 capital, 0.1% fees, 0.05% slippage), so both endpoints' submitted capital/fee/slippage/risk fields were accepted and then silently ignored -- confirmed this is the EXACT SAME bug class backend_app/routers/strategy_operations.py::_backtest_runtime_for's own docstring already names and fixes for the plain (non-optimization) backtest endpoint (that fix's own comment explicitly calls out get_backtest_runtime() by name as the thing it is NOT calling, for this exact reason) -- the optimize/walk-forward endpoints had simply not received the same fix. Fixed both call sites the same way: new backend_app/routers/strategy_operations.py::_optimization_engine_for(body) constructs a fresh OptimizationEngine() and a fresh BacktestRuntime(...) (from the request's own initial_capital/commission/slippage/risk_per_trade/max_drawdown/daily_loss_limit fields) per request; backend_app/routers/strategies.py's /walk-forward closure does the equivalent inline, reusing the values already read into its OptimizationConfig (so no duplicate payload.get() calls). get_optimization_engine()/get_backtest_runtime() themselves are UNCHANGED -- kept, not deleted, since tests/test_save_performs_no_backtest.py's Requirement-22.1 tripwire still needs to patch get_backtest_runtime by name in both router modules to prove a strategy SAVE never starts a backtest. Removed a redundant local re-import of OptimizationEngine/BacktestRuntime inside /walk-forward's closure that would otherwise have shadowed the module-level names and silently defeated test patching at the new injection points. New tests/test_opt03_optimization_engine_is_not_a_shared_singleton.py (6 tests, direct construction, no mocking -- mirrors tests/test_task_6_1_backtest_execute.py's existing proof pattern for the sibling bug): two calls return two different engine instances with independent _optimization_history (the concrete cross-tenant leak, reproduced then shown closed); the runtime carries the SUBMITTED capital/fee/slippage/risk values, not the class defaults; two different configurations produce two differently-configured runtimes; the engine returned is wired to THIS call's own runtime; the singleton accessors themselves are unchanged and still work (negative control). Updated tests/test_strategy_analysis_endpoint_accuracy.py's two walk-forward tests, which mocked get_optimization_engine/get_backtest_runtime by name, to patch the new injection points (OptimizationEngine/BacktestRuntime class constructors) instead -- both still pass. Full regression (opt03 + endpoint_accuracy + backtest_execute + validation_sweep + route_contract + router_registration_completeness, 441 tests) clean except the 2 unrelated pre-existing billing failures already confirmed earlier this session; tests/test_save_performs_no_backtest.py's pre-existing 10 failed/10 errored (an unrelated environment gap, confirmed identical on the pre-change baseline via git stash) are untouched by this fix.
findings.remaining_action: This closes the isolation half (OPT-03's own title and remediation note) for both call sites that exist. NOT attempted: OPT-02's separate, deeper finding that walk-forward analysis does not actually fit per-window parameters and reports several hardcoded placeholder figures -- a correctness question about the ALGORITHM, independent of this finding's isolation question, and out of this fix's scope.

findings.title: The dedicated websocket service (ws_server.py) is completely broken; a terraform apply of the existing ALB fix would take down all realtime
findings.evidence: INVESTIGATED THIS SESSION, deliberately NOT fixed. Confirmed the 'completely broken' half precisely: backend/event_publisher.py::EventPublisher (publish_order_filled/publish_position_updated/publish_pnl_update/etc, writing to Redis channels 'orders', 'positions', 'pnl', 'portfolio', 'signals', 'market_data', 'alerts', 'circuit_breaker') is never instantiated or called anywhere outside its own defining module (grepped the whole backend_app/ tree for EventPublisher()/get_event_publisher/publish_order_filled/publish_position_updated/publish_pnl_update -- zero hits outside event_publisher.py itself). backend/ws_server.py subscribes to exactly those channels and broadcasts whatever it receives to connected clients -- so it is wired correctly to a Redis bus that nothing in the real order/position/pnl code path ever publishes to. The REAL in-process realtime mechanism, confirmed by grep, is api_ws/ws_manager.py::ConnectionManager, used directly by paper_channel.py, paper_session_service.py, core/realtime_sync.py and routers/library.py -- an entirely separate, in-process path from the dedicated ws_server.py microservice. backend/dag_event_loop.py's own comment (task 14.2/14.3, Requirement 23.7) confirms this independently and from the OTHER direction: it documents that this method used to publish a signal-status frame via EventPublisher.publish_signal_trace, that ws_server.py's _redis_listener 'fans straight back out' under the Signal_Trace flat-broadcast channel, that this is an UNAUTHORISED-BROADCAST pattern Requirement 23.7 forbids (the channel 'names no owner and no deployment, so its subscribers are never authorised against the resource the frame describes'), and that task 14.2 REPLACED this emission with a per-deployment, authorised channel instead. Terraform confirms the deployment side is real, not just app-level drift: terraform/alb.tf defines aws_lb_target_group.websocket (port 8002, matching ws_server.py's own WS_SERVER_PORT) and aws_lb_listener_rule.websocket_rule (path /ws/*, priority 90); terraform/ecs.tf defines a full aws_ecs_task_definition.websocket + aws_ecs_service.websocket pointed at that target group. No .github/workflows reference exists to build or push the vyomquant-websocket image, consistent with this being built but never actually deployed through the current CI pipeline. THE REASON NEITHER OPTION WAS TAKEN: tests/test_task_14_3_legacy_broadcast_retired.py -- the test suite task 14.3 itself wrote when it performed the Requirement 23.7 replacement described above -- contains test_the_dedicated_ws_server_still_subscribes_to_it, which asserts the legacy channel remains in ws_server.CHANNELS, with the comment 'ws_server.py's fanout is the "any other consumer" the task protects.' This is a DELIBERATE, DOCUMENTED decision from that earlier task: it explicitly chose to leave ws_server.py and EventPublisher in place, unconnected to the new per-deployment channels, rather than delete them, on the stated reasoning that something outside that task's own scope ('any other consumer this spec does not cover') might still need the legacy flat-broadcast channel to exist. tests/test_websocket_auth_fail_closed.py separately exercises ws_server.py's OWN FastAPI app directly (4 tests: /ws/public/{channel} and /ws/{tenant_id} both fail-closed on no/invalid/mismatched token) -- so the SERVER's own authentication is itself already correct and tested, which rules out 'the server's auth is the broken part'. Deleting ws_server.py now would directly contradict task 14.3's own explicit decision without visibility into what that 'any other consumer' might be, and deleting it would break 6 existing, passing tests across two files that specifically pin its continued existence. Repairing it (wiring EventPublisher into the real order/position/pnl code paths) would mean duplicating what ConnectionManager already does in-process, for unclear benefit, and is exactly the kind of cross-cutting change to the live order-execution code path this session has consistently declined to improvise without a clearer mandate.
findings.remaining_action: NOT fixed. Deleting ws_server.py/event_publisher.py/the Dockerfile.websocket/the terraform websocket target-group+ECS-service+ALB-rule would break the DELIBERATE invariant tests/test_task_14_3_legacy_broadcast_retired.py pins ('any other consumer this spec does not cover') without knowing what that consumer is or whether it still matters -- that question needs an answer from whoever wrote or owns that decision, not a guess. Repairing it (wiring EventPublisher into the real order/position/pnl paths so it broadcasts real data) duplicates the in-process ConnectionManager path (api_ws/ws_manager.py) that paper_channel.py/paper_session_service.py/realtime_sync.py already use for the same purpose, for unclear benefit, and touches the live order-execution code path broadly enough that this session judged it unsafe to improvise. A dedicated session should: (1) confirm with whoever owns this area whether 'any other consumer' of the legacy flat-broadcast channel still exists in production; (2) if not, delete ws_server.py + event_publisher.py + Dockerfile.websocket + the terraform websocket resources (alb.tf's aws_lb_target_group.websocket/aws_lb_listener_rule.websocket_rule, ecs.tf's aws_ecs_task_definition.websocket/aws_ecs_service.websocket, outputs.tf's websocket_endpoint) together with the 6 tests that pin its existence; (3) if so, wire EventPublisher into the real event sources with the SAME per-deployment authorisation Requirement 23.7 already requires, not the flat broadcast it currently performs. EITHER WAY, this must happen BEFORE any terraform apply of an unrelated ALB fix that would newly route /ws/* traffic at a service that, as shipped, authenticates correctly but has nothing real to broadcast.

findings.title: Per-deployment execution-config limits (notional cap, position cap, slippage tolerance) are validated and stored but no execution path reads them
findings.evidence: Confirmed the defect exactly as named: deployment_binding.EXECUTION_CONFIG_FIELDS names five fields (max_order_notional, max_open_positions, slippage_tolerance_bps, order_timeout_seconds, retry_policy). normalise_execution_config's own docstring claims an unknown key is refused 'because execution_config is read by the execution path' -- grepped the whole execution path (BotRunner, ExecutionGuard, order_control, strategy_operations.py, strategy_service.py) for every one of the five field names and found NO reader anywhere; the only other occurrences are the field-name declaration itself and a docstring reference. A deployment with max_order_notional=1000 ran with exactly the same order-size ceiling (ExecutionGuard._validate_order_size's own process-wide self.max_order_size_usd, not anything per-deployment) as one with no execution_config at all -- a trader who set it believed a limit was in force that was not. Found and reused an EXACT precedent for the right fix already in this codebase: strategy_service.assert_deploy_params_applicable / DEPLOY_PARAMS_NOT_APPLIED already makes this same choice (fail loud, not silently discard) for capital/trade_size_pct/stop_loss_pct/max_drawdown_pct -- a prior pass of this same remediation effort, per that code's own comment block and its own regression file naming convention. Applied the identical pattern to normalise_execution_config: any of the five known fields supplied with a real (non-None) value now raises DeployRejected('EXECUTION_CONFIG_NOT_ENFORCED', ...), distinct from the pre-existing EXECUTION_CONFIG_UNKNOWN_FIELD refusal for a field that is not published at all. This surfaces identically at BOTH call sites that already route through this one normaliser: the preflight endpoint (as a failed, named condition plus deployable: False, discovered before submitting) and the deploy endpoint itself (the same refusal, now instead of a silent accept). None/absent and an empty execution_config document are unaffected -- only a real value on a known-but-unenforced field is refused. Updated three existing tests that had locked in the old, buggy behaviour as if it were correct: test_task_8_2_deployment_binding.py::TestExecutionConfig::test_the_designs_fields_are_kept (renamed and rewritten to assert the refusal, plus a new per-field sibling test) and its end-to-end TestBindingIsWrittenAsOneRow test (switched its execution_config payload from a real value to {}, which is what the test is actually about -- the OTHER binding fields reaching the row); test_task_8_2_deploy_preflight.py's test_a_known_execution_config_field_passes (renamed and rewritten to assert the condition now fails with deployable: False, the same way its own sibling test for an UNKNOWN field already did one test above it). Investigated the remediation note's first option (enforce in ExecutionGuard/BotRunner at order-construction time) and deliberately did NOT attempt it this pass: that is a change to the live order-validation hot path, with its own design questions (where does a per-deployment config reach ExecutionGuard from -- loaded by deployment_id? threaded through the signal? -- that the codebase does not currently answer anywhere) and needs dedicated testing against the live execution path rather than a same-session addition riding alongside a safety-tightening fix. New tests/test_deploy01_execution_config_fields_not_enforced.py (10 tests): each of the five fields refused on its own with the distinct code; all five together named in one refusal; the unenforced-field refusal is distinct from the unknown-field refusal; None/absent/empty are all still accepted. Full regression: new suite (10) + every deployment-binding/preflight/deploy-strategy test in the repo + validation_sweep (580+ tests) clean except pre-existing test-isolation flakiness independently confirmed unrelated (ran the SAME 6 tests with and without this change via git stash -- identical failures both times, same pass counts) and the 2 pre-existing billing failures already confirmed earlier this session.
findings.remaining_action: Real enforcement of these five limits inside ExecutionGuard/the bot runner at order-construction time -- the remediation note's other, harder option -- is NOT done. This pass closes the 'silently ignored' danger (a stored-but-inert limit a trader believes protects them) by refusing to accept a value for any of the five fields until an execution path actually reads it; it does not add that execution path. Needs: a design decision on how a per-deployment execution_config reaches ExecutionGuard/BotRunner at order time (deployment-id-keyed lookup vs. threaded through the signal), real enforcement code, and testing against the live order-validation path -- a larger, separate pass given the live-trading blast radius of touching that hot path.

findings.title: Six strategy-performance endpoints read QuestDB tables that nothing ever writes; they silently return zeros for every strategy
findings.evidence: Of the six strategy-performance endpoints (performance, equity-curve, monthly-returns, daily-returns, execution-metrics, risk-metrics), confirmed by reading backend/metrics_service.py directly that five already degraded honestly on no data (get_equity_curve/get_monthly_returns/get_daily_returns return [], get_execution_metrics/get_risk_metrics return {}) -- only get_strategy_performance's _empty_performance_metrics() fabricated a full dict of 0.0/0 values, indistinguishable from a strategy that genuinely traded and broke exactly even. Confirmed the root cause: strategy_performance/strategy_risk/executions have no writer anywhere in this codebase (grepped backend_app/ for any INSERT into them -- none), so this method is reached on every single call. Fixed by changing every QuestDB-sourced numeric field in _empty_performance_metrics() to None. Verified the 3 call sites of this method (routers/strategy_operations.py's passthrough handler, and backend/strategy_service.py's 3 internal callers) only embed the dict in a larger response with no arithmetic performed on its fields, so this change is safe. This is the backend half of the same defect FE-06 describes on the frontend side; both were fixed together since fixing one without the other does not change what a trader actually sees. New regression tests/test_metrics01_no_data_is_not_a_fabricated_zero.py (5 tests): every field is None on no data AND on a query exception (a QuestDB outage must not look like a clean sheet of zeros); a genuine zero in real data is NOT converted to unavailable; the other five methods are unchanged (regression guard).
findings.remaining_action: Not attempted (explicitly offered as the alternative in this finding's own remediation note, not chosen): implementing the actual QuestDB writer pipeline for strategy_performance/strategy_risk/executions. That is a substantial, separate feature build (deciding what writes these tables, at what cadence, from which part of the execution pipeline) and was judged out of scope for a P2 honesty fix. The honest-unavailable fix chosen here requires no such build and is the safer, immediately deliverable half of the finding's own two offered options.

findings.title: Marketplace browse builds a PostgREST filter from raw user input
findings.evidence: Confirmed by reading backend_app/routers/library.py::browse_library: the `q` search parameter was interpolated raw into a PostgREST or() filter string -- query.or_(f"name.ilike.%{q}%,description.ilike.%{q}%") -- and PostgREST's filter mini-language treats `,`, `.`, `(`, `)` as syntax, so a search term containing any of them could close the current clause and open a new one against an unrelated column. Separately, the handler fetched ALL matching rows via query.execute() and sliced [offset:offset+limit] in Python, so every browse request transferred the entire matching catalogue regardless of page size. Fixed both. (1) Extracted _postgrest_quoted_ilike_pattern(term): wraps the term in double quotes (PostgREST's own escaping rule), backslash-escaping \ and " themselves FIRST -- in that order, deliberately, since escaping quotes before doubling backslashes would let a trailing backslash absorb its own escaping backslash and leave the closing quote unescaped. findings.title: Exchange credential test endpoint is an unrestricted validity oracle for arbitrary third-party API keys
findings.evidence: Confirmed by reading backend_app/routers/exchange.py::test_connection (POST /api/exchanges/test): it dials the named venue with WHATEVER api_key/secret_key/password/uid the request body carries -- nothing requires those credentials to belong to the caller -- and had neither a route-specific rate limit nor require_aal2 (only the generic get_current_user), matching the title's own description exactly: an unrestricted validity oracle for third-party keys. Added @limiter.limit("10/minute") -- the same bound routers/auth.py already uses for account-enumeration-prone endpoints -- which bounds how many candidate keys a single caller can probe per minute, the dimension "unrestricted" names. require_aal2 was deliberately NOT added, despite this finding's own remediation note suggesting it "matching store_keys": AAL2 raises the one-time cost of acting under a given identity; it does nothing to bound how many probes that identity can run once stepped up, so against BULK third-party-key probing specifically (the actual threat this finding names) it is the wrong tool, while store_keys needs it because it PERSISTS a credential to the caller's own vault (AUTH-01's documented "Exchange API key mutation" case) -- test_connection persists nothing. Adding it would also directly contradict tests/test_auth01_require_aal2_is_wired.py::test_read_and_test_handlers_do_not_require_aal2, a PINNED regression from an earlier finding in this same remediation effort asserting test_connection must NOT require AAL2, per require_aal2's own "DO NOT apply globally" rule for a handler that submits credentials but persists nothing -- that decision was not re-litigated here. New tests/test_sec12_exchange_test_endpoint_is_rate_limited.py (3 tests): a static AST check confirms the decorator is on test_connection specifically; a real end-to-end test mounts the actual route function on a FastAPI app wired with the real in-process limiter object and exception handler (DEV_MODE resolves it to in-memory storage, no Redis needed) and proves the 11th rapid request from one caller is rejected while the first 10 reach the handler; a negative control proves two different callers (keyed via TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS + X-Forwarded-For) each get their own 10-request budget rather than sharing one.
