findings.title: Notifications are kept in an unbounded per-process dict with an O(n) idempotency scan
findings.evidence: Confirmed the defect exactly as named: backend_app/routers/notifications.py's _in_memory_notifications was a plain, unbounded module-level dict -- one entry retained forever for every notification ever created in this process's lifetime, across every tenant, whether or not it was ALSO durably persisted to Supabase (list_notifications always tries Supabase first and only falls back to this dict when Supabase has nothing, confirmed by reading it -- so a persisted entry's in-memory copy was pure, unbounded-growth dead weight). The idempotency check also did a full scan (`for existing_id, existing_data in _in_memory_notifications.items(): ...`) on every single create, so it got slower, not just memory-hungrier, as the dict grew. Fixed with (1) _MAX_IN_MEMORY_NOTIFICATIONS (env-overridable via MAX_IN_MEMORY_NOTIFICATIONS, default 5000) -- once exceeded, the OLDEST entries are evicted (plain dicts preserve insertion order in Python 3.7+, and no code here ever re-inserts an existing key, so the first key is reliably the oldest); (2) an O(1) idempotency index (_idempotency_index, keyed by (user_id, idempotency_key)) replacing the full-dict scan, kept in sync on insert, eviction, AND delete (both delete_notification and delete_all_notifications now route through a shared _forget_notification_locked helper instead of a bare `del`, so a deleted or evicted notification's idempotency key is freed for reuse rather than left dangling). New tests/test_hy04_notifications_memory_bounded.py (6 tests, using a shrunk cap via monkeypatch rather than actually inserting 5000+ rows) proves: exceeding the cap evicts the oldest entries first; a duplicate idempotency key for the SAME user returns the existing id without growing the store; the SAME key for DIFFERENT users does not collide; delete_notification and delete_all_notifications both clean the idempotency index, not just the dict; an evicted entry's idempotency key is freed for reuse. Updated tests/test_notifications_feature_e2e.py's state-cleanup fixture to also clear the new _idempotency_index between tests (it only cleared _in_memory_notifications before, which would have let the new index leak across runs in that file's own autouse fixture -- a miniature version of the exact unbounded-growth problem this finding is about). Full regression (new HY-04 suite + existing notifications e2e suite, 1 file/23+ tests + tests/test_validation_sweep.py, 388+ tests) clean except the 2 unrelated pre-existing billing failures already confirmed earlier this session (missing real Supabase service credentials in this sandbox).
findings.remaining_action: The finding's remediation note offered TWO options joined by 'and/or': cap the in-memory structure, OR make Supabase the source of truth with a visible degraded-mode indicator. This fix takes the first option in full (bounded growth, O(1) idempotency) -- the second option's 'visible degraded-mode indicator' (e.g. surfacing to the user or to ops when notifications are running on the in-memory fallback rather than Supabase) was NOT attempted; Supabase was already and remains the primary store attempted first on every write and read, so this is an observability nice-to-have on top of an already-correct fallback, not a remaining correctness gap.

findings.title: Referral payout debit and payout insert are two non-transactional writes with best-effort compensation; payout completion is unimplemented
findings.evidence: This finding has three asks; two are fixed this session, the hardest (full transactionality) is deliberately deferred. (1) 'fail closed on lock-acquisition error': confirmed backend_app/routers/referral.py::create_payout_request's lock-acquire except clause did `lock_acquired = True` on any exception -- fail OPEN. Traced through core/cache/redis_manager.py::SharedRedisManager.set(), which is itself deliberately fail-soft (swallows every exception and returns False, never raises), confirming this except clause is currently DEAD CODE -- but a landmine: RED-01's own remaining_action (still OPEN) proposes making redis_manager raise for exactly this class of safety-gate caller, and if that lands, this dead branch would silently come alive and reintroduce the double-spend race it exists to prevent. Changed to `lock_acquired = False` -- fail closed under either implementation. The wallet's own atomic conditional UPDATE (.gte('approved_balance_usd', ...)) remains the real correctness backstop regardless of this lock, confirmed by reading it: two concurrent requests race on the SAME conditional UPDATE, and Postgres serializes it row-wise, so only one can ever match: failing closed here only costs a confusing-but-safe 'please wait' on a genuine Redis outage, never a double-spend. (2) 'implement the pending->completed settlement step': grepped the whole file for the word 'completed' before this fix and found zero writes of it anywhere -- a payout request could be created and then sit in 'pending' forever with no code path to mark it done or refused. New PUT /api/referral/payouts/{id}/settle, admin-gated (get_admin_user) and running under the service-role client (get_service_supabase, via Depends -- confirmed referral_payouts and referral_wallets both carry an owner-only RLS policy, user_id = auth.uid(), so an admin's own JWT cannot read or write a payout or wallet belonging to the user being settled; this is the SEC-08 pattern this codebase already uses for platform actions on another tenant's rows). 'completed' requires an external reference (the operator attests they performed the transfer manually -- there is no outbound payment-rail integration anywhere in this codebase for referral payouts, only inbound Stripe/Razorpay webhooks, so this correctly does not claim to move money itself) and records processed_at. 'rejected' re-credits the wallet balance create_payout_request's own debit had already taken out, reading the CURRENT balance and adding back the payout amount (not blindly restoring a stale snapshot) -- without this, a rejected payout would leave the money permanently unaccounted for. An already-terminal payout (completed/rejected) cannot be settled again (409, via an optimistic .eq('status', <expected>) guard on the update, the same CAS style the debit itself already uses). New tests/test_ref01_payout_lock_fails_closed.py (2 tests): a lock-acquisition error refuses the payout (409) and -- the actual correctness property -- NEVER reaches the debit step at all. New tests/test_ref01_payout_settlement.py (6 tests): a non-admin is refused before touching the database; completing records the reference and does NOT touch the wallet; completing with no reference is refused (400) and does not mutate the payout; rejecting re-credits the wallet by exactly the payout amount; an already-settled payout cannot be settled again for either terminal status. Updated tests/test_validation_sweep.py with a MutatingRoute entry for the new endpoint (the sweep's own completeness check caught the omission) and fixed a now-stale comment in tests/test_referral_payout_debit_is_compensated_on_insert_failure.py's harness fixture that described the pre-fix fail-open behaviour. Full regression (referral payout lock/settlement/compensation + ref02 + validation_sweep + route_contract + router_registration_completeness, 403 tests) clean except the 2 unrelated pre-existing billing failures already confirmed earlier this session.
findings.remaining_action: NOT attempted: making the debit (referral_wallets UPDATE) and the payout INSERT truly transactional (a single Postgres statement/RPC, or a saga with a durable compensation record rather than a best-effort one that only logs CRITICAL on failure). This is the same class of architectural change as PAPER-05 (move multiple PostgREST writes into one Postgres function/RPC executed in a single transaction) -- a larger, separately-designed and separately-tested lift than this pass's time allowed. The EXISTING best-effort compensation (already in place before this session, re-verified unchanged by this session's own test run) already closes the worst failure mode -- a debit with literally no payout row and no trace -- by re-crediting on both 'insert returned empty' and 'insert raised', with a CRITICAL log carrying exact figures if the compensation itself fails. That is a real, durable (if manual) recovery path, not full atomicity.

findings.title: Unauthenticated referral-code validation endpoint returns another user's UUID; its own rate limiter is keyed on proxy address
findings.evidence: Confirmed two independent defects in backend_app/routers/referral.py::validate_referral_code (POST /api/referral/validate). A future session wanting real identity verification should switch to a dependency that decodes and checks the JWT itself (e.g. get_current_user) and reassess whether keying the rate limit on the caller's JWT sub (the remediation note's other suggestion) becomes meaningful once that holds.

findings.title: The sign-in page advertises two-factor authentication, but the OTP step is never server-enforced
findings.evidence: Confirmed the defect precisely in algo22-terminal/src/pages/AuthPage.jsx: supabase.auth.signInWithPassword succeeding is a COMPLETE Supabase sign-in, not merely a password check -- src/supabase.js configures the client with persistSession: true, so the SDK immediately writes a live, fully-privileged session into its own storage the instant that call resolves. The handler's own pre-existing comment ('DO NOT grant application access or persist session to sessionStorage yet') only ever controlled this APP's OWN sessionStorage bookkeeping; it never touched the session Supabase itself had already established. The 6-digit email-OTP step that followed (handleVerifyOtp, calling supabase.auth.verifyOtp) was therefore decorative for general account access: the password alone already granted a fully live session before the OTP screen was even shown. (require_aal2-gated routes, SEC-05/SEC-15 this same session, were never affected -- this flow never touches supabase.auth.mfa.*, so AAL stays 1 regardless; the exposure is to everything NOT behind require_aal2.) Fixed per this finding's third offered option: supabase.auth.signOut() is now called immediately after a successful signInWithPassword (and after signUp, for the identical reason if this project's email-confirmation requirement happens to be off), before the OTP screen is shown. New tests/unit/authOtpFe04.test.jsx (3 tests, vitest): signOut is called once the password check succeeds; signOut fires BEFORE signInWithOtp is dispatched (ordering, not just presence); the full flow still ends in a real session once verifyOtp actually succeeds -- this fix tears down the interim session, not the feature. Pre-existing auth_otp.test.jsx (23 tests across both auth suites) and the FE-01 suites still pass unchanged (59 tests total, vitest).
findings.remaining_action: This closes the gap for general account access via the password+email-OTP flow specifically. It does not and cannot make this a real, Supabase-tracked MFA factor (AAL2) -- that would require migrating to supabase.auth.mfa.enroll/challenge/verify (TOTP or phone), a materially larger change (new enrollment UI, recovery-code handling, a live Supabase project to test against) not attempted here. The sign-in page's 'two-factor authentication' copy is now true in the sense that a password alone no longer grants a live session -- it was not re-examined word-for-word against the stricter claim that this is AAL2-grade MFA, which it still is not.

findings.title: The API client overwrites caller-supplied Idempotency-Key headers with its own weak hash
findings.evidence: Confirmed by reading algo22-terminal/src/apiClient.js's request interceptor: it called generateIdempotencyKey(config.url, data), which hashed sessionId_url_payloadStr with a weak 32-bit simpleHash into the Idempotency-Key header UNCONDITIONALLY -- even when the caller (api/modules/strategies.js::deploy's options.idempotencyKey, a prepared but not-yet-wired-to-any-UI call site) had already set its own Idempotency-Key header, it was overwritten. The deeper bug: the hash was deterministic over (session, url, payload), so two SEPARATE, deliberately-identical submissions (placing the same order twice in a row on purpose) collided onto the identical key, and the backend's own idempotency check would then treat the second legitimate order as a duplicate retry of the first. Fixed: the interceptor now checks config.headers['Idempotency-Key'] for an existing value first and only falls back to its own generator when the caller supplied none; the fallback itself (generateIdempotencyKey) no longer takes url/data at all -- it is now idemp_${crypto.randomUUID()}, content-independent, so two identical submissions never collide. Removed simpleHash (now unused) and getSessionId (now unused -- confirmed no other call site anywhere in algo22-terminal/src or tests references either name). New algo22-terminal/tests/unit/apiClientIdempotencyFe05.test.js (4 tests, same axios-mock convention as the existing ATTACK 3 idempotency test it extends): a caller-supplied key is honoured verbatim, not overwritten; a request with no caller key still gets a defined idemp_-prefixed key; two identical submissions with no caller key get DIFFERENT keys (the collision bug, proven fixed); a GET request still never receives the header. The pre-existing tests/unit/attack_frontend_full.test.js (8 tests, whose ATTACK 3 only asserted the idemp_ prefix and definedness, not hash-determinism) still passes.

findings.title: The secret-redacting log filter is installed on only 13 marketplace/paper logger names; billing, exchange, execution and auth loggers are unfiltered
findings.evidence: Confirmed by reading backend_app/core/observability.py: RedactingLogFilter was attached only to the 13 logger names in GUARDED_LOGGER_NAMES (task 33.4's own scope: marketplace and paper) -- billing, exchange, execution and auth loggers carried no secret redaction at all. A Logger's own filters apply only to records it originates (Logger.handle checks self.filters, never an ancestor's), which is why attaching to 13 named loggers protected only those 13 and nothing else, however many other loggers exist in the codebase. Added install_root_log_redaction(), which attaches RedactingLogFilter to every HANDLER on the root logger instead -- a Handler's filters run for every record that propagates to it, whatever logger originated it, which is the mechanism the remediation note ("Install RedactingLogFilter at the root logging handler") names precisely. main.py calls it immediately after its own logging.basicConfig(...), which is what gives the root logger a handler to attach to. The original module's own docstring explains WHY root-handler attachment was avoided for task 33.4 ("redact the whole process's output, which the task forbids") -- that was a deliberate narrow scope for that task, not a permanent prohibition, and LOG-01 is exactly the later finding asking for the wider behavior that task declined. New tests/test_log01_root_redaction_covers_every_logger.py (4 tests, using a standalone logger/handler pair, never the real process root): an arbitrary, never-individually-guarded logger name is redacted once the handler it propagates to carries the filter; a record from an ALREADY-guarded logger (PaperRepository) is proven not to be double-mangled by passing through both its own logger filter and the root handler filter (the second pass on already-redacted text is a no-op); the installer is idempotent; a handler-less logger (the real root before basicConfig runs) returns 0 rather than raising. tests/test_log_redaction.py (362 tests, pre-existing) still passes; confirmed main.py still imports and boots with the root handler now carrying the filter.
findings.remaining_action: Covers the single root handler logging.basicConfig installs, the dominant real log path for this process (every logger with propagate=True, the default, eventually reaches it). Does not retroactively cover a handler some other module attaches directly to a non-root logger and removes from the propagation chain (propagate=False), nor a handler uvicorn or another framework might attach to the root AFTER main.py's own install_root_log_redaction() call runs -- neither case was found by reading main.py, but a dedicated audit of every logging.basicConfig/addHandler call site was not performed. Two pre-existing, unrelated test failures (test_exchange_credential_log_redaction.py's EXCH-01 sandbox-refusal mismatch, test_task_33_2_rate_limit_keys.py's rate-limit-count test) were confirmed to reproduce identically on the unmodified baseline via git stash -- not caused by this fix, not fixed by it either.

Fixed anyway, same reasoning as SEC-11 (a fail-open landmine in an unreached module becomes a live bug the moment something is wired up to call it): both except blocks now fail CLOSED specifically for the one rate-limit type/operation this module's own vocabulary ties to venue-ban risk (RateLimitType.ORDERS_PER_MINUTE / operation="orders"), matching the remediation note's own distinction, and fail open for the cosmetic/UI-facing types (signals, API calls, WebSocket connections) as the note explicitly says may remain acceptable. get_status() (read-only, "without consuming quota" per its own docstring, not an enforcement gate) and reset() (operator action) were left untouched -- neither is a decision point this finding is about. A future session should decide whether to delete backend_app/core/distributed_rate_limiter.py and the unused parts of exchange_rate_limiter.py entirely (ccxt's enableRateLimit already covers the real need with no distributed-coordination gap, since each pod throttles its own calls to the SAME per-pod ccxt client instance per exchange connection -- whether that is sufficient across multiple pods sharing one exchange account's global limit was not investigated here and is a separate, not-yet-tracked question), or wire DistributedRateLimiterIntegration into a real call site if genuine cross-pod coordination of exchange-venue calls is still wanted.

findings.title: Checkout currency/country detection trusts client-controllable headers, but the actual pricing impact is narrow
findings.evidence: Confirmed by reading backend_app/core/country_detection.py: extract_client_ip unconditionally trusted CF-Connecting-IP, True-Client-IP, X-Real-IP and X-Forwarded-For, and detect_country_from_headers unconditionally trusted CloudFront-Viewer-Country and CF-IPCountry -- a caller that reaches this process directly, bypassing whichever CDN is supposed to set these (this deployment's own terraform does not describe a CloudFront/ALB topology at all -- INF-02), could set any of them to anything and get a different region's price list via pricing_service.py::determine_pricing_context's IP-detection tier. Traced the actual commercial impact and confirmed the finding's own 'narrow' framing: determine_pricing_context's step 3 (an explicit currency_override query param) already takes highest precedence over IP/header detection, so a user can already pick any supported currency outright -- spoofing the geo header is a stealthier route to a capability that already exists overtly, not a new one. Fixed the header-trust half anyway, reusing the house pattern SEC-10 already built for this exact question ('is there a real proxy chain in front of this process') rather than inventing a second one: added client_address.trusted_edge_is_configured() (True only when TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS is a valid >=1 integer, the same fail-safe-by-default check trusted_client_address's own hop count already uses for rate-limit keys) and gated every one of the six headers above on it in country_detection.py. Unconfigured (this sandbox's default, and the fail-safe default for any deployment that has not explicitly confirmed its proxy topology), none of the six headers can change the detected IP or country any more -- detection falls through to the direct socket peer and the deterministic US/USD fallback. New tests/test_geo01_edge_headers_require_trusted_proxy.py (16 tests): trusted_edge_is_configured tracks TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS exactly as trusted_client_address's internal hop count does; each of the six headers is proven ignored with TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS unset, including the one case that actually matters commercially (a spoofed CloudFront-Viewer-Country against an unconfigured deployment resolves to US/USD, not the attacker-chosen country); a negative control proves every header still works once TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS is set, so this is a default, not a removal. Updated tests/test_billing_localization_e2e.py's five existing header-trust tests to set TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS (the deployment-has-confirmed-its-topology case they were already written to exercise) and added a new TestEdgeHeadersUntrustedByDefault class (6 tests) proving the previously-undefended default. Full tests/test_billing_localization_e2e.py + test_production_payment_e2e_acceptance.py + SEC-10/REF-02/SEC-12/validation_sweep/route_contract regression (399 passed) clean except the 2 unrelated pre-existing billing failures already confirmed earlier this session.
findings.remaining_action: The header-trust root cause is closed for every deployment that has not explicitly confirmed TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS -- which, per INF-02, describes this platform's actual production deployment today (no terraform describes its real topology, so there is nothing here to tell this code whether a CDN really fronts it). Once an operator sets TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS for the real topology, trust resumes exactly as before this fix -- a CloudFront origin-request policy that strips or validates these headers at the edge (this finding's own remediation note) is still the stronger, infrastructure-level fix and was not attempted: this session has no AWS credentials to configure CloudFront, and INF-02 already records that the repo's terraform does not describe the live distribution to configure a policy against. The remediation note's other half (keep FX rates fresher than the hardcoded baseline fallback) is a separate concern already owned by fx_service.py's own live-rate/cache/stale-grace/baseline tiers, unchanged here, and not re-verified in this pass.

findings.title: The admin-only portfolio-management API is largely non-functional (unawaited coroutines, nested-lock deadlock risk)
findings.evidence: The three asks in the original remaining_action (add missing awaits; fix the non-reentrant lock being re-entered; fix forced_reduction's close percentage) were the tip of a much deeper problem: this module (admin-only, mounted at /api/internal/portfolio-mgmt behind get_admin_user, confirmed separate from the real live-trading routers/portfolio.py) had ZERO prior behavioral test coverage anywhere in the repo, and crashed or hung at nearly every call site once actually exercised. Found and fixed, layer by layer, by actually calling the code rather than reading it: (1) validate_consistency() was called from both open_position and close_position but was never defined ANYWHERE on PortfolioManager -- AttributeError on every single open or close, before any other bug was even reached. Implemented it for real: checks each strategy's used_capital+available_capital==allocated_capital invariant and that open_positions/strategy_positions only reference live, correctly-filed positions. (2) Missing awaits on get_margin_metrics/_check_exposure_limits/register_strategy and several GET endpoints (exposure/margin/margin/health/margin/status/pnl/detailed-summary/prices/update) -- all returned unexecuted coroutine objects instead of data. (3) asyncio.Lock is not re-entrant: get_portfolio_summary held its own lock and then called three other lock-acquiring methods; open_position's conflict-cancellation step called the lock-acquiring close_position while already holding that lock; update_prices did the same into margin_monitor.check_margin_health -> _forced_position_reduction -> close_position. All three are guaranteed deadlocks the moment missing-await bug #2 is fixed first (which is presumably why nobody had hit this in whatever manual testing existed). Fixed by splitting get_margin_metrics/get_exposure_metrics/get_pnl_summary/_check_exposure_limits/close_position into `_locked` bodies the caller can invoke directly while already holding the lock, with public async wrappers that acquire it fresh; narrowed update_prices' own lock scope so the margin check and any resulting forced liquidation run after the price-update lock is released. (4) get_exposure_metrics built an ExposureMetrics() instance and then read/wrote MarginMetrics-shaped fields on it (margin_used, margin_level, margin_call_threshold...) that ExposureMetrics does not declare as fields at all -- AttributeError on every call where margin_used<=0, i.e. an EMPTY portfolio, the ordinary starting state. This was a copy-paste of the margin calculation onto the wrong dataclass; rewrote it to populate ExposureMetrics' own real fields (symbol/strategy exposure breakdown, gross/net/long/short exposure, leverage, concentration), which is also the shape every caller (get_portfolio_summary, create_snapshot) already assumed when reading .symbol_exposure/.gross_exposure off the result. (6) MarginMonitor's forced-liquidation path called self.pm.close_position(position_id=..., close_price=..., reason=...) -- but close_position's parameter is named exit_price, not close_price -- TypeError on every forced liquidation. Fixed, and made check_margin_health/_forced_position_reduction/get_margin_status async so they can properly await the manager calls they depend on (they were plain sync methods calling async methods, which can never actually run the async body). (7) the liquidation log said 'reducing by 25%' while the code's own comment admits there is no partial-close method and it always closes the entire position -- an operator reading logs during a real margin event would see a false 'only trimmed 25%' when 100% was actually liquidated. findings.remaining_action: True partial position reduction (closing e.g. 25% of a position's size rather than always closing 100%) is NOT implemented -- PortfolioManager has no partial-close primitive (resizing a Position's quantity while keeping it open and correctly re-deriving its realized/unrealized PnL split) and adding one is a real feature, not a bug fix, with its own design and test surface. This pass fixed the DISHONESTY (claiming 25% while doing 100%) and the crashes/deadlocks around it, not the missing feature -- always closing fully on a liquidation-risk margin event is a conservative, safe behavior, not an unsafe one, so this is a legitimate deferral rather than a masked defect.

findings.title: Two independent sequence allocators for paper session events can collide and drop a bar on feed disconnect
findings.evidence: Confirmed the collision mechanism exactly as named: paper_market_feed.FeedHandle._emit_feed_disconnected allocated its sequence from paper_repository.next_session_event_sequence (max(paper_events.sequence) + 1, read off the LOG), while every other Paper_Channel event (paper_events.record_event -> next_sequence -> paper_repository.allocate_session_event_sequence) allocates from an atomic compare-and-swap on the paper_sessions.event_sequence COUNTER. Traced the actual failure mode: the feed writer's INSERT (via insert_session_event) advances the LOG but never touches the COUNTER, so a subsequent ordinary event's counter-based allocation can read a stale, lower number and collide with the sequence the feed writer already used; uq_paper_event_seq then refuses that ordinary event's INSERT with PaperDuplicateSessionEvent, and neither paper_session_service._emit nor the bar-stepping loop that calls it catches or retries that exception -- so the bar is dropped, not merely delayed. Fixed by routing _emit_feed_disconnected through allocate_session_event_sequence instead, so there is only one source of truth for the next sequence number and the race cannot happen at all. next_session_event_sequence itself is kept (it has its own direct test coverage and tests/property/test_paper_channel_sequence.py reuses it as a synthetic log-based second writer to stress-test the counter allocator's retry logic in general) -- only its one production caller moved. Along the way, fixed a stale property test harness bug this change exposed: tests/test_paper_market_feed_selection.py's shared _session_row() fixture never carried an event_sequence key at all, and the fake client's eq-filter compares str(row.get(col)) against the literal given -- an ABSENT key reads back as 'None', which never equals '0', so allocate_session_event_sequence's own compare-and-swap would lose all three attempts against this fixture even though the real column defaults the row to exactly the value the swap expects. Seeded it at 0 (the column's real DEFAULT per migration 009), which is behaviourally transparent to every other reader (the allocator's own code already treats an absent/NULL value as 0) and only matters for this exact-string-equality fake match. Updated the two stale docstring claims in test_paper_channel_sequence.py that called next_session_event_sequence 'task 24.4's feed writer's allocator ... a real production path', which is no longer true after this fix. New tests/test_paper06_feed_disconnect_shares_the_allocator.py (3 tests): an AST check that the feed-disconnect writer's own source calls allocate_session_event_sequence and not next_session_event_sequence (catches a revert even without a live collision); a real disconnect advances the counter to exactly match the log's own highest sequence (they can no longer diverge); and the exact scenario this finding describes -- a disconnect immediately followed by an ordinary event -- allocates consecutive, non-colliding sequence numbers end to end, with both rows landing. Full regression: the new suite + every paper-trading test in the repo (tests/ -k paper, 1590 passed) + test_validation_sweep.py (373 passed), clean except 2 unrelated pre-existing EmptyCategoryError collection failures (confirmed pre-existing and unrelated earlier this session, e.g. test_dag_hash_sensitivity.py) and the 2 unrelated pre-existing billing failures already confirmed earlier this session.

findings.title: Backtests, optimization trials and walk-forward windows ran on the most recent bars regardless of the requested start_date/end_date
findings.evidence: Discovered while investigating OPT-02 (walk-forward does not fit per-window parameters): confirmed the root cause is upstream of optimization_engine.py entirely. backend_app/backend/backtest_runtime.py::run_backtest logs start_date/end_date and stamps them onto the backtests row's metadata, then calls self.data_engine.fetch_historical_ohlcv(symbol=symbol, timeframe=timeframe, limit=10_000, max_retries=3) with NO date-range argument at all. backend_app/backend/data_seeking_engine.py::fetch_historical_ohlcv had no date-range parameter to pass -- with since=None it always answers 'the most recent N bars', per its own docstring. Grepped every start_date/end_date usage in backtest_runtime.py and confirmed neither is used to filter/select data anywhere. Consequence: a backtest requested over 2020 and one requested over 2023 fetched and ran on byte-identical data (whatever was most recent when called); every optimization trial, Monte Carlo run, sensitivity run and benchmark comparison inherited the same defect through the one shared run_backtest call; and a walk-forward window's train and test periods -- different date ranges by construction -- ran on that same identical data, which is what made genuine per-window parameter differentiation (OPT-02) structurally impossible regardless of how the optimization logic itself was fixed. Fixed by adding a second, optional since_ms/until_ms mode to fetch_historical_ohlcv (a new _fetch_ohlcv_bounded that pages FORWARD from since_ms, trimming rather than rounding past a page straddling until_ms) while leaving the existing no-argument 'most recent' mode completely untouched -- the existing DATA-01 regression suite (7 tests) still passes unmodified. Wired run_backtest to use it via a new _requested_window_ms(start_date, end_date) helper that converts the two ISO strings already received into (since_ms, until_ms), with an unreadable/blank date falling back to (None, None) -- the prior 'most recent' behaviour -- rather than a new failure mode. New tests/test_bt02_backtest_honors_requested_date_range.py (13 tests): the bounded fetch's exact-window, multi-page, mid-page-trim and open-vs-closed-window-warning behaviour; _requested_window_ms's ISO/naive-UTC/blank handling; and two end-to-end wiring tests proving run_backtest actually calls fetch_historical_ohlcv with the window implied by start_date/end_date, including that two DIFFERENT requested windows are passed two DIFFERENT bounds -- the exact guarantee OPT-02's per-window fit now depends on. Full regression: the untouched-path DATA-01 suite plus 10 other backtest/optimization test files (224 passed total).
findings.remaining_action: None at the code level for the data-fetch mechanism itself. This finding only makes per-window / per-date-range backtesting POSSIBLE; it does not itself change optimization_engine.py's walk-forward logic to actually use different windows for fitting -- that is OPT-02's own remaining scope, tracked separately. Also not addressed: fetch_historical_ohlcv's 10,000-bar cap could still truncate a very wide requested window silently (it already warns via the existing under-coverage path when the window is open-ended, but a closed window wider than the cap is trimmed to its first bars with no warning, by design, since a closed window's own date bound is what the caller asked for) -- not flagged separately since it matches the existing cap-and-warn contract this function already had for the no-range mode.
